entities.name: Richard de Fournival
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Richard de Fournival (c. 1201 – 1260) was a prominent 13th-century French polymath, scholar, and trouvère, serving as Chancellor of the Cathedral Chapter of Amiens from 1246 until his death. Hailing from Picardy, his significance in medieval intellectual history stems from his diverse contributions across natural philosophy, optics, alchemy, and particularly, literature, where he innovatively blended scholastic inquiry with the conventions of courtly love. His work provides a crucial window into the intellectual ferment of Northern France during a period of burgeoning cathedral schools and nascent universities.

His most celebrated literary achievement is the *Bestiaire d'amour* (c. 1250), a unique allegorical prose bestiary that reimagined the traditional moralizing format by applying animal characteristics to the dynamics of romantic pursuit and persuasion. Beyond this, he authored the *Conseil d'Amours*, a collection of love letters, and the pseudo-Ovidian *De vetula*, a complex work touching upon alchemy, astrology, and autobiographical elements. Fournival was also a serious scientist, contributing to optics with his *Speculum astronomiae* and engaging with the burgeoning field of alchemy. Crucially, he amassed one of the largest private libraries of the medieval period, containing over 200 manuscripts across various disciplines, including classical texts, scientific treatises, and contemporary works.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Richard de Fournival's innovative *Bestiaire d'amour* profoundly influenced the allegorical genre in medieval literature, and his vast library became a cornerstone for the University of Paris, impacting intellectual development for centuries.
